title: JP Morgan’s Nigeria expansion to boost foreign investment — IMPI - Vanguard News
content: The Independent Media and Policy Initiative (IMPI) has said the planned expansion of global financial giant JP Morgan Chase into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector could attract fresh foreign investments, improve corporate financing and strengthen the country’s access to international capital markets.Nigerian travel guide The policy think tank said the American financial institution’s application for a national merchant banking licence was a significant endorsement of Nigeria’s investment prospects and could encourage more multinational corporations to commit long-term capital to the country.Nigerian travel guide In a policy statement signed by its Chairman, Dr Omoniyi Akinsiju, IMPI said the proposed expansion could reshape Nigeria’s corporate finance landscape by making it easier for businesses to access funding, structure large-scale projects and manage risks associated with cross-border investments. According to the group, JP Morgan’s transition from a representative office to a fully licensed merchant bank would enable it to deepen its involvement in trade finance, corporate lending, cross-border underwriting and other sophisticated financial transactions. It said the development could be particularly beneficial to capital-intensive sectors such as energy, telecommunications and manufacturing, where high borrowing costs and complex financing arrangements had continued to constrain investments. “JP Morgan Chase’s move to secure a national merchant banking licence in Nigeria marks a significant shift in West Africa’s corporate finance landscape,” IMPI said. The group added that the proposed operations could help multinational companies structure investments more efficiently through direct access to cross-border trade facilities, commodity hedging instruments and syndicated financing involving domestic and international markets. It said the availability of such services could reduce delays and additional costs businesses often encounter when relying on multiple financial intermediaries to execute major projects. IMPI also argued that Nigeria’s sovereign and corporate borrowers could benefit from stronger links to international capital markets, while the presence of a major global financial institution could reinforce confidence among foreign pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and private equity investors. However, the think tank cautioned that JP Morgan’s proposed entry would not automatically translate into increased foreign direct investment, stressing that the broader benefits would depend on prevailing investment conditions and the consistency of economic policies. The policy group attributed renewed international interest in Nigeria to the economic policy direction of President Bola Tinubu’s administration, particularly the foreign exchange market reforms and removal of petrol subsidy introduced in 2023. It acknowledged that the reforms initially triggered inflationary pressures and currency depreciation but argued that they had helped reshape the country’s external financial position and renew international investor interest. “Our analysis found that the near four years of the federal administration mark a record of consistent current account surpluses, underpinned by an aggressive strategy to not only drive FDI but also link it to domestic macroeconomic stability with a medium- to long-term microeconomic impact,” the statement said. IMPI maintained that the reforms represented a structural shift from policies that previously distorted market signals towards a system intended to improve price discovery, strengthen external balances and attract sustainable investments. It said the emerging challenge was to convert renewed international interest and short-term capital inflows into investments that would expand productive capacity, create jobs and strengthen the real economy. The think tank also identified a potential shift in Nigeria’s foreign investment profile, arguing that the country could gradually move away from excessive dependence on foreign portfolio investments towards more sustainable foreign direct investments. It explained that portfolio investors had been attracted by high yields on government securities and other short-term financial instruments, while the Central Bank of Nigeria’s monetary and foreign exchange policies sought to address currency pressures and rebuild investor confidence. It noted that the surge in portfolio inflows had helped boost Nigeria’s foreign reserves to more than $55 billion, although the high interest rates associated with the strategy had also increased borrowing costs for domestic businesses. “For nearly two years, foreign capital prioritised government debt and Treasury bills (FPI) over physical infrastructure (FDI) because short-term paper yielded safely above 25 per cent,” IMPI said. The group argued that as inflation moderates and yields on fixed-income securities decline, investors could become more interested in longer-term opportunities, including infrastructure concessions, industrial projects and direct equity investments. It added that the declining attractiveness of short-term financial instruments could encourage institutional investors and cross-border private equity firms to redirect some of their funds towards productive assets. “For our standpoint, as inflation begins to moderate, the focus is shifting towards converting these temporary portfolio flows into permanent, factory-to-market FDI,” the statement added. IMPI said JP Morgan’s proposed merchant banking operations could facilitate this transition by providing the financing structures and risk-management instruments required to execute large-scale investments. It argued that international investors required more than favourable policy announcements before committing capital to physical projects, noting that predictable financing arrangements, credible risk-sharing mechanisms and access to institutions capable of handling complex transactions were equally important. The group said the presence of a globally influential financial institution could help bridge that gap by connecting Nigerian businesses and projects with international capital providers. It added that improved access to corporate finance could support investments in energy infrastructure, telecommunications and industrial production, while making it easier for Nigerian companies to participate in international trade. However, IMPI said the broader impact would depend on the consistency of economic reforms, the evolution of borrowing costs and the ability of businesses to translate improved financing opportunities into viable projects. It maintained that JP Morgan’s proposed expansion should be viewed not merely as the arrival of another financial institution, but as an opportunity to deepen Nigeria’s integration into global investment networks. The group said the ultimate test would be whether renewed investor attention translated into factories, infrastructure, expanded production and jobs rather than remaining concentrated in short-term financial instruments. For Nigeria, it added, the opportunity lay in converting improving investor sentiment into sustained capital formation capable of supporting long-term economic growth. title: Market Coverage Cites No J.P. Morgan Target as BTC Trades Near $77K - Bitcoin Foundation
content: J.P. Morgan Bitcoin price prediction coverage cites no bank target; BTC trades near $77K as ETF outflows and election uncertainty shape the news. The J.P. Morgan Bitcoin price prediction search turns up no bank target in market coverage around November 3. CoinGecko lists Bitcoin at $77,435, down 0.05% in 24 hours. Coverage instead tracks political uncertainty, ETF withdrawals and moves by other financial firms. Bitcoin’s current price is context, not a J.P. Morgan forecast. And because a separate Solana token also uses the BTC▼$76,338.00 ticker, readers should check which asset a quote refers to. The market coverage around this date contains no J.P. Morgan price target, forecast or analyst rationale. That does not prove the bank has never published a Bitcoin forecast elsewhere. There’s no sourced J.P. Morgan number here to compare with Bitcoin’s current price, or to present as the bank’s 2026 or 2027 target. Before treating a headline or social post as a bank forecast, check it against a J.P. Morgan publication or a clearly attributed statement. Coverage centers on Bitcoin trading near $77,000, uncertainty around the US midterm elections and recent outflows from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. It also covers Citi’s ETF pitch to wealth clients and planned institutional custody service—Citi activity, not a J.P. Morgan prediction. BitGo has separately added Stacks Bitcoin staking to qualified custody for eligible institutions. As The Defiant describes it, the arrangement pairs BTC with STX▲$0.3199 worth 5% of a Bitcoin position for roughly six-month bonds funded by Stacks miners. It’s a custody and staking development, not a price target. The $77,435 quote is for Bitcoin, which CoinGecko identifies as BTC. It ranks as the largest cryptocurrency in that listing, with a market capitalization of about $1.56 trillion and 24-hour trading volume of roughly $27.8 billion. Those figures belong to Bitcoin’s market, not every token carrying the BTC ticker. A shared label alone doesn’t make two listings the same asset. A separate token named BTC is listed on Solana. It has one Raydium trading pair and a recorded creation date of May 14, 2026. Its listed price is $79,828.48—not the Bitcoin price discussed above. The listing has no website or social links. It doesn’t identify the Solana token as native Bitcoin or show an affiliation with Bitcoin’s network or J.P. Morgan. A shared ticker is no reason to assign it Bitcoin’s history, supply rules or reputation. Search results, exchange interfaces and token trackers may show a name or ticker before readers check the underlying asset. Here, the distinction is between Bitcoin and a separately listed Solana token—not two interchangeable Bitcoin prices. Check the asset name and network shown by the market venue before relying on a quote. That matters especially when a bank-forecast search leads to a token page: the Solana listing offers no evidence of a J.P. Morgan connection. Satoshi Nakamoto created Bitcoin in 2009 under a pseudonym. Bitcoin is a decentralized cryptocurrency, not a network operated by a bank or company. Bitcoin.org describes it as an open-source payment network. Its design supports peer-to-peer transactions without a bank acting as intermediary, while a distributed system maintains the network’s rules. Bitcoin uses proof-of-work mining and the SHA-256 cryptographic algorithm. Those are features of its network, not of the separate Solana token listing. That distinction matters when banks make headlines. A bank discussing custody or an investment product is talking about how clients access or hold Bitcoin; it isn’t changing the underlying network or guaranteeing a price. Bitcoin’s maximum supply is 21 million coins. Programmed halvings, roughly every four years, reduce miner rewards. Both rules are built into the native Bitcoin network. Scarcity is part of how investors assess Bitcoin, but the supply schedule doesn’t say what BTC should trade for on a particular date. It isn’t a J.P. Morgan price prediction. CoinGecko’s November 3 listing puts Bitcoin at $77,435, with a market capitalization of about $1.56 trillion and 24-hour volume of approximately $27.8 billion. The figures refer to Bitcoin, not the separate Solana token. This is a dated reference for the price-prediction search, not a year-end estimate. Bitcoin can move after the timestamp; its price alone doesn’t show what a bank expects next. Bitcoin fell 0.05% over 24 hours in the November 3 listing—a small daily move, not a sharp sell-off. Its latest price was near the $77,000 area covered in that day’s market reporting. Bitcoin/USD circled $77,000 at Tuesday’s Wall Street open, while the same account put a recent local low near $76,300 on Friday. That $76,300 level is a reference point, not a guaranteed floor. A current quote and a recent low show where Bitcoin traded. Neither gives a future target, and the coverage around November 3 attaches no J.P. Morgan forecast to either level. A useful forecast comparison needs a named author or institution, a publication date and a stated time horizon. Without those details, don’t attribute a number circulating with the phrase “J.P. Morgan Bitcoin price prediction” to the bank. On Tuesday, market coverage described investors weighing the US midterm elections and the possibility of a shift in the balance of power in Congress. That uncertainty formed part of the broader trading backdrop; it wasn’t a Bitcoin-specific announcement. The account also noted a tech-stock rebound as Wall Street trading began. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had closed Monday down 0.5% and 1.1%, respectively, as investors weighed political questions and company news. Bitcoin held near $77,000 in the Wall Street-open coverage, after local lows around $76,300 the prior Friday. Those levels offer a recent range to watch, but neither is guaranteed to hold. The story is about market context and trading levels, not a new bank forecast. Shifts in equity sentiment or political expectations could change market conditions, but the coverage doesn’t quantify a specific effect on Bitcoin’s next move. Watch whether Bitcoin stays around the recent $76,300 low and the $77,000 trading area, and whether the political uncertainty in the coverage eases or intensifies. These are observation points, not targets. A 0.05% 24-hour decline is too small to call a crash or a rally. A stronger prediction would need more evidence—a clearly identified forecast or a new market catalyst, for example—not an extrapolation from one day’s move. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $398.62 million in outflows on November 2 and $643 million on October 30, according to BeInCrypto. The article also put combined Monday outflows from US Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs at $538 million. These are fund withdrawals, not a J.P. Morgan forecast. ETF flows offer a demand indicator to watch alongside Bitcoin’s price, but the figures alone don’t explain why investors redeemed or where BTC will trade next. Citi Wealth has pitched spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs to suitable clients as investments that could sit alongside stocks and bonds. Its October report cited regulatory clarity, institutional adoption and crypto’s low long-term correlation with traditional assets, while also outlining risks and suitability limits. Citi said in August that its Custody+ platform would begin institutional Bitcoin custody later in 2026. The stated timing was “later this year,” with no specific launch date in the account. That’s a Citi service plan, not a J.P. Morgan price outlook. More than one token uses BTC or Bitcoin in its name. The Solana listing is one example; its single Raydium pair and token name don’t make it native Bitcoin. Check the network and asset identity before interpreting a quote or acting on it. The listing’s missing website and social links call for caution when identifying the project, but they don’t prove fraud, backing or a rug pull. The token record lists about $7.98 billion in liquidity alongside just $1.26 in 24-hour volume. Those figures don’t establish active trading depth or assure holders they could exit at the displayed price. That means companies often get bogged down by manually moving between systems and matching data, time that could be spent on higher-value strategic efforts. title: JPMorgan Kinexys: How Should Banks Use Blockchain? - Tiger Research Reports
content: JPMorgan is the world's largest dollar-clearing bank, handling $12 trillion a day, and its blockchain unit Kinexys is building products to process these payments around the clock. The Blockchain Deposit Account (BDA), which lets corporates move funds at any hour, is its main product, with estimated daily volume of about $3.5 billion, or roughly 0.03% of JPMorgan's total payments, assuming BDAs still account for half of Kinexys's total volume. JPM Coin, which turns deposits into tokens, has recorded only 48 transfers on Base since its first issuance, and the intraday repo service, which lends funds for a matter of hours, has not disclosed figures since 2022. JLTXX, a tokenized fund, by contrast reached $800 million in net assets within two months of launch, most likely because stablecoin issuers placed their reserves in it. The results are still small, but JPMorgan is gradually expanding its blockchain business on the foundation of the payments clients and deposits it already has. JPMorgan is the world's largest dollar-clearing bank, processing roughly $12 trillion a day across 120 currencies. Its payments business posted record revenue of $19.3 billion in 2025 and, in the third quarter of 2026, generated the most revenue of any business within the Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), firmly establishing it as one of the group's core sources of revenue. JPMorgan has recently been moving its core payment rails onto blockchain to automate payment processing, run it around the clock, and improve efficiency, and Kinexys sits at the center of that shift. Kinexys is both an internal business unit and a key platform. Its roots date back to a blockchain research group established in 2015, and it took its current name in November 2024. Kinexys aims to build financial infrastructure that is "programmable, always on." Its goal extends beyond individual tokenization projects to infrastructure on which deposits and assets move on a single ledger around the clock and settle automatically according to preset conditions. Kinexys brings together blockchain-based payments, asset tokenization, and services and capabilities developed through Liink and Kinexys Labs, across private and public blockchain networks. Dive deep into Asia’s Web3 market with Tiger Research. Be among the 23,000+ pioneers who receive exclusive market insights. Kinexys's main service is the Blockchain Deposit Account (BDA). It is a deposit account on a blockchain operated by JPMorgan, designed so that corporates can move and settle funds 24 hours a day without being tied to banking hours. This works because of how the ledger is structured. Transfers between BDAs only change balances within the same JPMorgan-operated ledger, so they settle immediately, including at night and on weekends, without waiting for banking hours. BDAs also support programmable payments that move funds automatically once set conditions are met, as well as on-chain FX. Using Kinexys BDAs, EBANX reduced the time needed to transfer funds between its accounts across roughly 20 countries from more than a day, caused by country-specific processing times and intermediary steps, to a few minutes. Because settlement happens in real time within JPMorgan's ledger, EBANX can confirm receipt regardless of time zone, which has allowed it to reduce the buffer funds it holds in each account. According to a 2025 report Kinexys published with the MIT Digital Currency Initiative, BDAs processed more than $1 billion a day. Kinexys's total daily volume at the time was over $2 billion, meaning BDAs alone accounted for half of its transaction volume and were a major contributor to its activity. JPMorgan has not disclosed BDA figures separately since then, but Kinexys's total volume has grown steadily. Average daily volume rose from more than $5 billion in 2025 to roughly $7 billion in July 2026. Assuming BDAs still account for about half of the total, as they did in January 2025, current BDA daily volume can be estimated at about $3.5 billion. Even including repo, these figures remain small relative to JPMorgan's overall payments volume. Kinexys's total daily volume of $7 billion is about 0.06% of the payments business's daily volume (roughly $12 trillion), and the BDA estimate of about $3.5 billion is about 0.03%. BDA is a commercial service through which real corporate funds already move. Compared with JPMorgan's overall payments volume, however, it is still at an early stage, used mainly by a limited number of companies to move funds between their own entities. Its volume continues to grow, which indicates that the service is proving useful. JPM Coin (JPMD) turns BDA deposits into tokens on public blockchains. The aim is to let deposits that were previously usable only among JPMorgan clients be used on blockchains outside the bank. A company issues JPM Coin from its BDA balance, uses it to pay for transactions on Base or Ethereum, and can later redeem the tokens for funds credited to its BDA. Ownership is restricted, however, since only wallets approved by JPMorgan can hold the token. JPMorgan's goal is to settle public-chain transactions directly in bank deposits. Until now, institutions that wanted to pay in dollars on public chains have mostly had to use stablecoins. B2C2, which took part in testing at launch, expected JPM Coin to provide "real-time, onchain settlement with the assurance of a regulated USD deposit" for the same reason. JPMorgan has not, however, quantified the resulting cost savings. On-chain data shows the following issuance and usage of JPMD by chain. Base: Since the first issuance in June 2025, there have been only 48 transfers, and none at all since February 20, 2026. Outstanding supply as of November 3 is about $1 million, roughly 0.02% of USDC supply on the same chain (about $4.3 billion). Ethereum: No tokens have been issued on the Ethereum version launched later, and no clients beyond the initial testing participants have been identified as actual users. Contrary to expectations, JPM Coin has seen almost no real use, despite being issued across 2025 and 2026. Given that BDA took about three years to establish real use cases, however, JPM Coin is still at a very early stage and could begin to see broader adoption in early 2027. Digital Financing is an intraday repo service that lets institutions borrow for a matter of hours against Treasuries. Financial institutions such as banks and broker-dealers sometimes need funds for only a few hours during the day to meet payment obligations. Digital Financing lets them obtain short-term funding at a lower rate than a bank's intraday credit line. The borrower sets aside Treasuries and the lender sets aside cash, both in tokenized form, and the two are exchanged simultaneously at the agreed time. Because maturity can be set to the minute, the borrower pays interest only for the time used, and the cash leg is funded through BDAs. This has lowered borrowing costs. According to a JPMorgan case study, one global financial institution cut its borrowing rate by 56% by using Digital Financing instead of a bank intraday credit line. The problem is that it is hard to verify whether the service is still used at that scale. In a 2022 report, JPMorgan stated that cumulative repo volume had exceeded $430 billion since the service launched in November 2020, but it has not published repo figures since. Broadridge's DLR, a competing blockchain repo platform, averaged $359 billion in daily volume as of September 2026. Even measured against JPMorgan's 2022 figures, DLR's daily volume alone exceeds half of JPMorgan's cumulative volume at the time, a substantial gap in scale. ICMA also named DLR and Kinexys as blockchain repo platforms that have reached commercial scale, while assessing that JPMorgan's impact on the overall market remains limited. These tokenized funds represent shares in J.P. Morgan Asset Management's money market funds (MMFs) as tokens on public blockchains. They were created to bring institutional money held on public chains into JPMorgan funds. Stablecoin issuers are the main institutions holding large sums on public chains. For every $1 of stablecoins issued, an issuer must hold $1 in safe assets such as Treasuries as reserves, and many place these reserves in MMFs to earn interest. The problem is timing. Stablecoin holders can ask to redeem their coins for dollars on-chain even on a Saturday night, but ordinary MMF shares exist only as entries on the fund manager's books and cannot be sold or moved until business hours resume on Monday. Tokenized funds leave this register in place and issue an equivalent number of tokens on the blockchain, with Kinexys keeping the register and the token supply in sync. Issuers can therefore hold reserves as MMF tokens and earn interest while still being able to move them on-chain immediately when needed, including at night and on weekends. On-chain token transfers do not necessarily mean immediate cash redemption or an immediate transfer of legal ownership, however, since legal ownership of fund shares follows the fund's register of investors. JLTXX, which JPMorgan launched in May 2026, also targets this demand and was designed for use by stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. Its prospectus states that stablecoin issuers are expected to hold the fund's shares as part or all of their reserve assets. JLTXX launched with $100 million from JPMorgan, and its net assets grew to $800 million by the end of July, two months later, according to SEC filings. As of November 3, on-chain supply across Ethereum and Solana totaled about 795 million tokens. The buyers of JLTXX have not been named. SEC filings as of the end of September show that depository institutions such as banks hold about 84% of shares of record and non-financial companies hold about 16%. Taken together with the design purpose stated in the prospectus, this suggests the money most likely came from stablecoin issuers or the banks that hold their reserves. JLTXX's rapid growth does not mean it is clearly ahead of the market. As of the end of September, JLTXX ($628.5 million) was similar in size to competitor Franklin Templeton's on-chain fund ($668 million) and still well behind BlackRock's BUIDL (about $2.08 billion), according to rwa.xyz. The market JLTXX targets, however, is only beginning to grow. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has projected that the stablecoin market, currently about $300 billion, could grow tenfold by 2030 under the GENIUS Act, and the amount issuers already place in MMFs is substantial. Circle, the issuer of USDC, held about $62.5 billion, roughly 84% of its reserves, in a single dedicated government MMF as of the end of September, about 80 times JLTXX's current size. If JLTXX wins reserve mandates from issuers one at a time, it could grow to several dozen times its current size. The stablecoin market, however, stood at about $295.5 billion in November, roughly where it was a year ago, so it remains to be seen when this projection will materialize. JPMorgan has invested across the firm for more than a decade, starting with a blockchain research group in 2015 and moving through Onyx to today's Kinexys. Backed by a firmwide technology budget of more than $15 billion a year, it has fully integrated blockchain into the core infrastructure of its payments business. CEO Jamie Dimon openly acknowledged at Investor Day that "we spent too much on it," which shows that JPMorgan's commitment has gone well beyond basic R&D. This sustained commitment of resources and investment clearly distinguishes it from other financial institutions. In 2026, JPMorgan has emphasized a new direction, stating that "we need to roll out our own blockchain technology" to compete with new blockchain competitors. It has also said that blockchain will eventually replace traditional financial infrastructure, and it is putting more weight behind practical service expansion through Kinexys, including crypto-collateralized lending and the launch of public on-chain MMFs. Kinexys's decade offers clear strategic lessons for traditional financial institutions adapting to changes in financial infrastructure. Rather than building a new chain without a clear purpose or launching standalone services with little substance, JPMorgan started from the strengths of its core business: its existing payments clients, for whom it processes $12 trillion a day, and its deposit ledger. It first proved the efficiency of its internal infrastructure through BDA, including 24/7 real-time settlement and transfers between affiliated entities, and then expanded step by step into on-chain markets with products such as JLTXX. Many financial institutions face pressure to deliver quick results. JPMorgan's blockchain business, however, has developed over more than a decade, building on its deposit ledger, liquidity, and existing payments clients. For institutions developing their own blockchain strategies, the lesson is to start with established strengths and expand through practical use cases. title: 200 days into the frontier: What we know and what to do now - JPMorganChase
content: See how our clients and partners—from small business owners to workforce training leaders—work with JPMorganChase to drive meaningful impact and economic growth where they live and work. Veteran’s Unconventional Path to Landing her Dream Job in Tech U.S. Army Veteran Ashley Wigfall transitioned to a civilian role and charted her path to technologist through mentorship and skills training at the JPMorgan Chase tech hub in Plano, Texas. Chairman and CEO Letter to Shareholders By the JPMorganChase Global Technology Leadership Team More than 200 days into the Super Intelligence era, the implications for business are becoming clearer. Technology is accelerating offense and complexity faster than many enterprises can reduce accumulated risk. Capabilities once limited by specialized expertise are becoming more accessible. Vulnerability discovery and attack automation are moving at warp speed. Remediation is not. At the same time, the frontier’s rapid advancement is increasing dependence on hardware, data centers, telecommunications, water and power. We are all increasingly interconnected, which means resilience ultimately depends on how well the whole ecosystem works together. Earlier this year, we shared 10 actions that enterprises can take to strengthen cyber resilience. Those actions remain important foundations. What is now clearer is that AI magnifies risks accumulated over time. Complexity itself has become a security risk. We are already seeing that critical vulnerabilities can trigger urgent, large-scale remediation efforts. Technology that is outdated or unsupported can become a liability overnight. And as companies race to deploy AI agents, security has to advance with it. For CEOs, the imperative is clear: Change assumptions, shorten decision cycles and build resilience. Reduce accumulated technology risk while ensuring that products and infrastructure being built today are secure and resilient by design. Practices and risks that were acceptable in a former technology environment may no longer be tolerable. When technology and threats move faster, tolerance for avoidable risk has to change too. Outdated technology, internet-facing systems and remediation timelines designed for a slower environment can become liabilities with little warning. Leaders need to reset risk appetite, make exceptions explicit, fund the necessary change and establish accountability across product, technology, security, operations and suppliers. That does not mean treating every problem as equally urgent. It means acting decisively where exposure and potential impact are greatest and directing resources accordingly. Challenge the notion that stable technology is safe technology. Software or hardware can continue to operate while becoming progressively harder to protect. When vendors or software maintainers stop supporting older technology, security patches will stop too. This is known as end of support (EOS). EOS is predictable. Accepting the risk is a choice. PHP illustrates the issue. When serious vulnerabilities emerged, security fixes were provided only for the current version. Organizations running older versions had to move to current or remove the dependency. The same principle applies to unsupported programming platforms, open-source libraries, operating systems and aging hardware. Unsupported technology should be treated as a time-sensitive business liability. Any exception should have an accountable owner, funding, compensating controls and a dated exit plan. Start with a complete, current inventory of software and hardware. Then prioritize by asking three questions: Keeping perimeter technology patched is necessary, but not sufficient. Firewalls, virtual private network gateways and other remote-access technologies connect internal systems to the internet. Because they are directly reachable, a serious vulnerability can give attackers a path into the enterprise. Recent Citrix vulnerabilities underscored that risk, but the architectural issue extends beyond any single product. Patching the vulnerability in front of you addresses today’s exposure. If critical technology remains directly exposed to the internet, the next vulnerability can recreate the same risk. Companies should reduce direct exposure and add layers of protection. An independent authentication layer can prevent unauthenticated traffic from reaching the underlying service, making vulnerabilities harder to discover or exploit. This graphic is divided into two stacked panels that compare system security before and after adding an Auth Filter. The top panel, labeled "Without an Auth Filter," shows the system itself acting as the front door. Two figures, employees and customers on one side and attackers and AI-driven scanning on the other, both have a direct open path to a single box labeled "Internet-facing system," which contains an exposed sign-in page and applications and data. A caption notes that anyone on the internet can reach the sign-in page, and one unpatched flaw there can open a path into the enterprise before anyone has signed in. The bottom panel, labeled "With an Auth Filter," inserts a new middle layer between users and the system. This middle box, titled "Independent security layer at the edge," contains three sequential steps: Screen (block known attacks, floods, and bad bots), Verify (sign in with multi-factor authentication), and Authorize (allow only approved people). Employees and customers pass through this layer via a verified, private link to reach a separate box on the right labeled "Protected system," which is hidden from the internet and contains the same sign-in page and applications and data, now marked as unchanged behind the layer. Attackers and AI-driven scanning are shown being stopped at the edge, with a dotted line indicating that direct connections to the system are refused. Below both panels, three summary callouts state the benefits of this design: less exposure (the system cannot be reached directly from the internet), an independent layer (a flaw in the system alone is not enough to get in), and no single point of failure (the layer is built with redundancy and a tested fallback). In a technology environment, architecture is one of the company’s most consequential security decisions. Product speed and security should not be presented as opposites. Security and resilience requirements should inform market launch, scale and partner selection before architecture becomes difficult or expensive to change. Management teams should understand how a product could be attacked or misused, limit unnecessary access, protect sensitive data and test security throughout development. Unresolved material risk should have clear ownership. Frontier technologies are moving from answering questions to taking action. Agents can increasingly interact with enterprise systems, access information and execute tasks with limited human involvement. Capability, however, should not automatically determine authority. Before expanding what agents can do, establish what they cannot do. Access should be based on the task, not on the theoretical reach of the model. Human oversight should be proportional to consequence: a reversible, low-impact action warrants a different control than moving money, changing production systems or communicating with a customer. Frontier technology is compressing the time between vulnerability discovery, potential exploitation and the need to respond. Governance must be able to move at the speed of the threat. Speed does not mean bypassing governance or accepting uncontrolled change. It is the product of governance designed before the crisis begins. Traditional escalation paths, approval processes and change windows can become risks if they prevent an organization from acting quickly enough. During a significant event, the relevant decision-makers should be clear, escalation thresholds understood, emergency authorities defined and required evidence available quickly. Companies also need the ability to test and deploy critical fixes safely and at speed. Teams should not have to invent a decision process during the incident. Leaders must also be prepared to reprioritize. When new exposure materially changes potential impact, planned work needs to give way and resources need to move with the risk. Risk acceptance should be owned and time-bound. An organization may decide in hours and still require days or weeks to act. It may need to establish which systems are affected, locate accountable owners, test a patch, secure a change window, coordinate suppliers, deploy across a complex estate and confirm that remediation succeeded. Decision speed and execution speed require separate measures. Faster approval has little value if asset data is incomplete, testing capacity is constrained or deployment cannot scale safely. Both the operating model and the technology estate must support rapid action. CEOs should ask whether cyber incident-response teams have the access and authority to act at the speed of an attack, or whether they depend on layers of coordination and approval. When a critical service is exposed and cannot be fixed, teams may also need clear authority to isolate it or take it offline to prevent greater harm. Even the strongest internal process depends on technology suppliers to identify vulnerabilities, communicate them quickly and make fixes available. A supplier can determine how quickly the company responds. Companies should know which providers could become rate-limiting dependencies, whether notification and escalation expectations are contractual, and what options exist if a timely fix is unavailable. An affected service may need to be isolated, replaced or operated temporarily in a reduced state. Exercises should test more than whether a technical team can apply a patch. They should test whether the enterprise can establish exposure, provide executives with decision-useful information, activate emergency authorities, evaluate competing business impacts and deploy safely at scale. Companies cannot predict or prevent every technology disruption. Resilience is the ability to absorb a shock, maintain critical operations and recover with confidence. Every digital service ultimately depends on something physical: hardware, data centers, telecommunications, water and power. AI is increasing dependence on, and demand for, this infrastructure. At the same time, attacks, geopolitical events, energy constraints, supplier concentration and long hardware replacement lead times can create additional points of failure. Companies should understand where single points of failure exist: critical dependencies whose loss could disrupt an essential service without a readily available alternative. That could be a data center, source of power, telecommunications provider, critical hardware component or supplier. The question is whether the business could continue operating if one suddenly became unavailable. Cyber and physical resilience can no longer be managed separately. The disciplined response has three steps: identify the dependency, evaluate the business impact of its loss and act where the potential impact warrants it. Not every dependency requires full duplication. Investment should reflect potential impact, recovery objectives, replacement lead times and the practicality of alternatives. The CEO’s role is to ensure that the largest concentrations are visible and that accepted exposure is deliberate Continuity plans cannot compensate for architecture that allows one weakness, supplier failure or infrastructure disruption to put critical operations at risk. Resilience must be built into products and services, then proven through testing. Design critical services to contain failure, preserve essential functions and recover without relying on the component that failed. Use segmentation and containment to limit impact, build redundancy where warranted, design for graceful degradation and establish viable alternatives that can be activated within the required business timeframe. Then test it. Plans and executive assurance do not demonstrate resilience. Testing does. Exercise failover and recovery under realistic conditions and prove that critical operations can continue, data can be restored and used, and alternate systems, providers or facilities can carry the required workload. Testing should expose where reality falls short of design: how long recovery actually takes, which services miss their targets, what constraints emerge and what remains unresolved. The goal is not to prove that disruption can always be prevented. It is to prove that the company can take a hit, keep its most critical operations running and recover with confidence. The pace will not slow. More capable models will accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation. As these capabilities become more widely available, the volume and complexity of cyber and technology events will increase. Organizations must change with the environment. There is no room for complacency. Assumptions, timelines and controls that worked before need to evolve. Reset the tempo. Identify material risks early, understand the potential impact and be prepared to shift priorities and resources when the risk changes. Move faster on what matters most. The organizations that succeed will not be those that predict every threat. They will be those that reduce accumulated risk, make decisions faster, contain failures when they occur and recover before disruption becomes a crisis. Tier 1 — What AI changes: AI is not necessarily the crisis itself, but it changes how fast, how far, and through what a crisis can spread. Four boxes lay out the underlying shifts: Speed (vulnerability discovery is accelerating, but remediation is not), Autonomy (AI agents gain access and authority without equal certainty they will act as intended), Scale (risks that once seemed tolerable can become material quickly), and Dependency (more reliance on hardware, data centers, telecom, water and power). Tier 2 — The CEO response: Three connected black-headed panels linked by arrows show sequential flow. Each panel ends in a boxed "CEO question" prompting a specific leadership check: which assumptions were formed for a world that no longer exists, what would stop the company acting within hours if a material vulnerability emerged tomorrow, and what evidence shows critical services can continue or recover when something fails. Below the three panels, a dashed feedback loop connects all three back to a single rounded callout reading "Learn and adapt: change the control, architecture or decision process that failed," indicating the framework is cyclical rather than linear. Tier 3 — Summary band: A black summary band with three short headers restates the overall intent: Reset the tempo (identify, prioritize and address material risk faster), Adapt decisively (shift resources, tolerances, controls and architecture), and Prove it (show the company can take a hit and keep operating). A closing italic line beneath the graphic reinforces the theme: every action ends in a CEO evidence request, asking management to show it, not assure it. title: The S&P 500 may be headed for 'outsized gains' despite tech-stock rout, JPMorgan says - Business Insider
content: Amid a brutal week in the tech sector, the S&P 500 is flashing one sign better days are coming: improving market breadth. The tech sector is still getting pummeled by fears around AI, but JPMorgan Private Bank sees one bullish signal in the benchmark index that suggests the market is soon headed for a rebound. In a recent note, strategists at the bank pointed to increased market breadth, a measure of the number of winning stocks relative to losing stocks in the S&P 500. For a long time this year, breadth has been narrow, with just a few big names driving the gains at the index level while the majority of stocks struggled. The percentage of stocks in the index that have hit a new 20-day high has risen to over 50%. It's the first time market breadth has risen that high since the second quarter of 2025, around the time the market was making a historic comeback after the tariffs-fueled market crash. The extent to which market breadth has increased recently has historically been followed by more gains in the market over the next three-month and six-month periods, the bank added. JPMorgan recently lifted its year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,000, implying 5% upside to the index's current levels. "Despite a crowded risk calendar, breadth and historical outperformance sets the US stock market up for outsized returns after the midterm elections," Kriti Gupta, an executive director and global investment strategist in JPMorgan's private bank arm, and Nick Roberts, a portfolio manager at the bank, wrote in a note on Friday. It's been a rough few weeks for US stock investors, with the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 on track to end October in the red amid several rounds of heavy selling in the AI trade. Fears around AI capex have been widespread and run in multiple directions: investors worry that Big Tech firms may be spending too much on artificial intelligence, and, on the other hand, fear that a pullback in spending could trigger a cascade of consequences that will crush suppliers in the data center space. Deteriorating market breadth was one of the first warnings investors got that not all was well with the AI trade. Several weeks ago, the benchmark indexes were hovering near record highs, but more than 80% of the S&P 500 had slipped into correction territory. The breadth decline was interpreted by strategists as damage building up underneath the market's surface. Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. More analysts are eyeing a market as the market moves closer to the midterm elections, which has historically been a clearing event that allows stocks to renew their rally once its over. In the six months after the midterms, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 14% since 1970, according to an analysis from BlackRock. In the meantime, the tech sell-off continued on Friday as investors balked at Amazon's and Intel's latest earnings reports, with both tech giants signaling that capex spending would increase next year despite negative cash flow. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down around 8% from its October peak. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, meanwhile, has plunged 28% from its 2026 high, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF is down 43% from its latest peak.

title: The 'haunted' housing market's real problem may be too few people, not too few homes, says J.P. Morgan’s David Kelly - Fortune
content:
“The housing market is haunted,” according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else. The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren’t showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that “implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year,” compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century. That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn’t built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly’s read is that the country is “still in a situation of net excess supply.” Thursday’s GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, “marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters.” But “the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending,” he said. In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall. Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold “regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections,” because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill. Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units. Buyers have thinned out. The National Association of Home Builders’ measure of buyer traffic fell to 18 in October, its lowest level since April 2012 excluding the start of the pandemic, and 43% of builders cut prices. Kelly expects housing starts of 1.32 million this year, the weakest since 2019, falling to 1.24 million in 2027. Others see demand cooling, too. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies said in June that household growth “has slowed sharply” and that reduced immigration is expected to dampen housing demand further. A Mortgage Bankers Association white paper projects 8.6 million new households from 2025 to 2035, down from 10.1 million in 2010 to 2020. Fewer buyers haven’t meant cheaper mortgages. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.32% last week, according to Freddie Mac. Kelly notes that’s below its 50-year average of 7.68%. From January 2008 to December 2021, the rate averaged just 4.15%. “It is important to recognize that this period was the anomaly, rather than today,” he writes, and there’s “little reason to believe that mortgage rates will fall much below 7.0%” without a recession. Kelly said he expects the Fed to raise rates in December and thinks weak housing could make that the last hike of this cycle. What would change his mind, he told Fortune, is if “wage growth suddenly picked up,” or if inflation expectations priced into Treasury inflation-protected securities “were to rise significantly.” Builders are squeezed from both sides. Construction workers are hard to find, Kelly writes, and wages in the industry are rising faster than elsewhere, partly because of the swing in immigration and partly because data-center construction is competing for the same workers. Tariffs and the same infrastructure boom have pushed up the cost of materials. Kelly told Fortune it’s hard to put a number on how much the AI boom is adding to the cost of building a home. But spending on data centers rose 73% in the year through August, to an annual rate of $85 billion, he said, and “it is likely that the resource squeeze from data centers will intensify in 2027.” The ghosts are hardest on the young. Homeownership has fallen since 2022, Kelly writes, “with a much sharper recent decline for those under age 35.” He calls it a decline that is “postponing the reasonable aspirations of young people to be able to marry, settle down and build a family in their own home.” Asked whether that drop is mostly about mortgage rates, Kelly pointed elsewhere. “I think it is a combination of tougher lending standards and the reality that older households have had more of a chance to accumulate a bigger down payment,” he said. That call can be viewed as being very pessimistic about Bitcoin, as it's far lower than its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 43.9% over the last four years, or as bullish, as it implies that it'll outperform every major asset class the bank models over a fairly long period of time. Both figures are broadly in line with the historical data. Using J.P. Morgan's figures for the coin's estimated forward returns versus stocks, the two earn the same 0.32 points of return above holding cash per point of volatility. That implies it does not really believe there will be a higher volatility-adjusted return with Bitcoin than with stocks, only that Bitcoin's higher expected return comes with proportionally more risk. The subtext here is that if you can't handle seeing the value of your investment swinging around a lot, Bitcoin is not going to be pleasant for you to hold even if it ultimately returns more. The factor at the heart of the projection is Bitcoin's shrinking rate of new supply being mined over time, versus the generally expanding global money supply. J.P. Morgan called the coin "a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing," meaning it's a risky asset that tends to do well when central banks expand the money supply. That mostly fits; while the coin hasn't proven it's an effective hedge against inflation, its strictly limited supply and the impossibility of printing more of it by fiat should mean its purchasing power continues to hold up over time. Per J.P. Morgan, this is the first time this report series has included a Bitcoin return forecast. It still doesn't recommend an allocation. Still, it expects Bitcoin to beat stocks over the next decade. So it's worth owning at least a little, once your traditional portfolio is sufficiently diversified. As for how much to buy, BlackRock found in December 2024 that a 2% Bitcoin allocation in a traditional 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio accounted for 5% of its total risk, while a 4% allocation accounted for 14%. Morgan Stanley, on the other hand, suggested in late 2025 that the most aggressive portfolios should hold at most 4% in the asset. That argues for an allocation of less than 5% for most investors -- and remember, if the coin's inherent volatility is going to make you lose sleep, aim for the shallower end of that pool with your allocation.
